description: During each club meeting a Topicsmaster poses a random prompt and members deliver a 1-2 minute impromptu speech on the spot, with no preparation. The canonical impromptu/quick-wit drill of the format.
Deliver a 4-6 minute speech introducing yourself to the club on any topic; the first Pathways project.
Present a 5-7 minute speech on a narrowly-defined topic with clear purpose and organization.

exercise_name: Introduction to Vocal Variety and Body Language
description: Give a 5-7 minute speech with evaluation focused specifically on vocal variety or body language.
Deliver two 5-7 minute speeches where the second incorporates feedback from the first, plus serve as an evaluator for another member. Builds the feedback-loop habit.
Present a 5-7 minute speech that includes at least one humorous anecdote or story.
Deliver a 5-7 minute speech on an unfamiliar topic while monitoring and adapting to live audience reactions.
Give two 3-4 minute social speeches such as toasts, eulogies, acceptance speeches, or praise speeches.
Present a 5-7 minute speech that is or includes an established story, personal narrative, or fictional tale.
Present a 5-7 minute speech using detailed, vivid sensory descriptions of the topic.
Fulfill the Topicsmaster role at a meeting, then comment on each Table Topics speaker to demonstrate active listening.
Give a 5-7 minute speech on your humor perspective including at least one anecdote.

exercise_name: Power of Humor in an Impromptu Speech
description: Present two 2-3 minute impromptu speeches with humorous anecdotes related to randomly assigned topics. Combines impromptu speaking with humor.
Conduct a 5-7 minute role-play interview at a club meeting, fielding questions in character.
Present a 5-7 minute speech while responding live to role-played audience disruptions and heckles (12-15 minutes total).
Deliver a 5-7 minute speech followed by an unscripted audience Q&A (15-20 minutes combined). Practices thinking on your feet.
Present a 5-7 minute speech intended to inspire and motivate listeners.
Write and present an 18-22 minute keynote-style humorous speech (Level 5 capstone).

Tell a true, personal 5-minute story (max 6) on the night's theme, from memory with no notes, on stage in front of an audience. Ten storytellers are drawn at random and scored 1-10 by audience judge teams.

exercise_name: Know Your Story By Heart (not memorized)
description: Practice telling your story from a bullet-point outline rather than a memorized script, so delivery stays natural and conversational without notes.
Before telling, identify what you stand to gain or lose and why the events matter to you; rework the story until the stakes are explicit.

exercise_name: Start in the Action / Craft the Opening Line
description: Rewrite the opening so it begins mid-action with a first line that both sets up the stakes and grabs attention immediately.
Identify the moment of change that separates a story from an anecdote: how the teller's world or perspective is different at the end than the beginning.
Card game mode: everyone at the table responds to the same drawn theme card and its prompts with their own personal story.

exercise_name: A Game of Storytelling (Getting to Know You)
description: Card game mode: each player draws their own theme card and shares an individual story based on it.

exercise_name: A Game of Storytelling (Best in Show)
description: Card game mode: teams of two exchange stories from a card, then present their favorite to the larger group.
Card game mode: a host draws a card, players pitch their story using only three key words, and the group votes on which story to hear in full. Mimics the live StorySLAM at home.
Education-program framework: develop 'seed ideas' for where stories might be hiding, then orally draft the story aloud before writing it down.

provider: Stanford GSB / Matt Abrahams — Think Fast Talk Smart
description: Point at or look at objects in the room and call each one anything except what it actually is (a window becomes 'cat' or 'fireplace'). Trains spontaneity and disarms the inner self-evaluator. Used to open his Stanford class.

provider: Stanford GSB / Matt Abrahams — Think Fast Talk Smart
description: Build a personal pre-speaking plan (greet anxiety, reframe, breathe, use present-tense self-talk) to manage nerves before impromptu moments. A repeatable preparation drill.

provider: Stanford GSB / Matt Abrahams — Think Fast Talk Smart
exercise_name: Structure with a Framework (problem-solution-benefit / what-so what-now what)
description: Practice answering an on-the-spot question by routing the response through a memorized structure such as 'problem, solution, benefit' or 'what / so what / now what' to stay concise and memorable.

provider: Stanford GSB / Matt Abrahams — Think Fast Talk Smart
description: Printable exercises practiced in everyday low-stakes settings (emails to coworkers, chats with friends) so spontaneous-speaking skills are rehearsed before high-stakes moments.

provider: Stanford GSB / Matt Abrahams — Think Fast Talk Smart
description: Self-reflection drill working through the six steps: manage anxiety, prevent perfectionism, stay open-minded, listen actively, structure content intentionally, and stay succinct/focused/compelling.
A group builds a single coherent story one word per person around the circle; trains listening and letting go of control.

exercise_name: Word at a Time Scene / Expert
description: Players perform a scene, or answer as an 'expert', generating each sentence one word at a time between participants.
A scene is performed in which every line must be a question; whoever fails to ask a question or hesitates is out. Trains quick verbal wit.
Build a scene where each consecutive line of dialogue must start with the next letter of the alphabet.
Rapid-fire word association around a circle; each player instantly says the first word the previous word triggers. Warm-up for spontaneity and letting go of self-censoring.
Each response must begin with the final letter of the previous word or line. Word-agility drill.
Build an exchange where each line rhymes with the prior one; trains rapid verbal invention under constraint.
Group tells one story; a conductor points at a player who must continue seamlessly, and any hesitation, repetition, or grammatical slip means 'die' (they're out). Storytelling under pressure.

exercise_name: Three Sentence Story / String of Pearls
description: Players collaboratively assemble a narrative in tightly constrained chunks (three sentences each, or connected 'pearl' segments filling in a beginning and end).
One improviser plays a (secret) famous character and fields rapid questions from the rest as reporters, answering in character without breaking. Trains thinking on your feet.
A host guesses the secret identities/quirks of guests through improvised interaction at a party. Character and quick-response drill.
Players perform in gibberish 'foreign language' while others provide live subtitle translation or dubbed voices. Trains spontaneous narrative invention and tonality.
Improvisers spontaneously create and pitch an advertisement for a random or suggested product. Persuasion and quick invention.
Players 'throw' a word to each other while keeping a verbal/physical pattern going; warm-up for focus, listening and quick response.

provider: Speak Up Storytelling podcast (Matthew & Elysha Dicks)
description: A 5-minute daily practice: each day ask 'if I had to tell a 5-minute story about today, what would it be?' and write one or two lines capturing the most storyworthy moment in a spreadsheet. Builds a personal story bank and trains noticing.

provider: Speak Up Storytelling podcast (Matthew & Elysha Dicks)
description: Take a prompt (a place, object, or experience) and recall when you had your first, last, best, and worst of it; each cell is a potential story seed. Also playable as a conversation/icebreaker game.

provider: Speak Up Storytelling podcast (Matthew & Elysha Dicks)
description: Timed nonjudgmental free-writing session: write continuously, jumping between ideas without editing, to surface unexpected story material and connections.

provider: Speak Up Storytelling podcast (Matthew & Elysha Dicks)
description: Each episode Matt and Elysha take a real story (often a listener's or a recent telling), then break down structure, stakes, the moment of change, and delivery, modeling a feedback loop listeners can imitate.

Free live online drop-in class (weekdays 4pm ET) where participants build collaborative comedy scenes and receive expert feedback after each scene; beginner exercises by default, advancing if the group is ready. Specific drill names not published.
Participants improvise short two-person comedy scenes and an instructor gives targeted feedback at the end of each scene, a rep-plus-coaching loop.
